The word you're looking for is "fungible". The dictionary defines it as "being of such nature or kind as to be freely exchangeable or replaceable, in whole or in part, for another of like nature or kind." What this means is that it acts as a placeholder.

Example:

I want an apple, but don't have the means to grow them. You have apples. I ask for one. You're not just going to give me an apple because you need them for your family and you worked hard to grow and pick them. So, you tell me that I can pick apples for an hour and you'll give me a few of them. I tell you I can't pick apples, but I can paint fences. Your fence is already painted, so no apple for me. Even if I could pick apples, I would need hundreds of different skills for the hundreds of things I might want to acquire. Not everyone needs painted fences.

But, we have this fungible stuff called money. So I agree to give you ℧5 that I earned for painting a fence last week for three apples. So, I have indirectly painted a fence in exchange for apples, by using money as a fungible intermediary. In fact, as long as there are fences to paint, I can get all the goods and services I need.

In regard to "money as debt," we get to thank something called "fractional reserve banking" for that.

So now you have all this money, but your house is not a safe place to put it. Now I've opened up something called a bank. Give me your money, I'll keep it safe, and give you an extra 5% per month. Meanwhile, I've taken the ℧1000 you've deposited with me and lent it out to others who need money, at 10% per month. It's good for both of us because I make money, and you do too. The problem is if you want to take out your ℧1000 and I don't have it. This is rare, though. Where it gets to be a problem is when I decide that, even though I only have ℧1000 in my bank, I'll lend out ℧2000, and hope the interest gets paid back before you need your ℧1000 back. So, where did that extra ℧1000 come from? Nowhere. It doesn't exist. No work was performed, no goods were sold, and no agency issued it. That "money" is debt.

And now it's gotten to the point where almost every government issues debt rather than money. The Federal Reserve bank in the US lends money to the US government, who then pays back the loan (with interest) by collecting taxes. The only value the money has is based on how much faith the citizens have in the government. It's great if you're the USA or the UK. Not so great if you're Zimbabwe. People lost faith in the money there, and it became worthless in a very short time. There are legitimate arguments both for and against faith-based currency, and I'll leave others to explain those. To sum up, money is almost exclusively debt in modern times, but that is not money's only or natural state.
